newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends off in US as trading gets underway in '97.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends off in US as trading gets underway in '97.

text.p: The dollar ended slightly lower after signs of solid economic growth caused stocks and bonds to tumble on the first trading day of the year, experts said.

"The dollar is not having any real strong direction because the asset markets are certainly more defensive as we go into the new year because Fed policy is looking not quite so certain as people thought it was going to be in December," said Tom Benfer, director, foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal in New York.
Benfer noted that some investors had suggested in December that the Fed might have to lower rates.
The National Association of Purchasing Management index unexpectedly rose to 54 in December from 52.7 in November. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, expected a December reading of 51.5.

The surprisingly strong data pressured stocks and bonds, which had also tumbled on Tuesday after reports showed new homes sold at a brisk rate in November and consumers surveyed in December were feeling decidedly upbeat about the economy.
Initially, the Dow industrial average had sank almost 100 points but staged a recovery to end down about six points.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond closed 1-6/32 weaker at 96.30/32 to yield 6.74 percent.
The dollar followed stocks and bonds lower but also staged a recovery that left it marginally lower. It slid to intraday lows of 1.5380 marks and 115.30 yen.
The U.S. currency, however, ended at 115.60/70 yen, down from 115.68/78 yen at the open. Against the German unit, the dollar fell to 1.5430/40 marks from 1.5445/55 marks.
The British pound or sterling, which soared on Tuesday to $1.7163, its highest level in more than four years, lost ground to several currencies on Thursday.
Sterling closed at $1.6933/43, down from $1.7040/50 at the open.

Anne Parker Mills, a foreign exchange analyst at Lehman Brothers, attributed the pound's weakness to political worries in Britain, technical factors in the foreign exchange market, a sharp drop in Britain's purchasing manager's index and thin market volume which exaggerates price action.
The Purchasing Manager's Index dipped to 52.5 percent in December from a downwardly revised 54.2 in November.
The pound's steep losses against the mark had also helped weaken the dollar, experts said.
In late dealings, sterling traded around 2.6067/77 marks, down sharply from about 2.6345/55 marks in early activity.

"When it falls against the mark as quickly as this, some people will sell sterling against the dollar and then they will sell dollars against the mark to lock in a sterling-mark sale," said Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
Foreign exchange trading was closed on Wednesday for the New Year holiday. Volume remained light on Thursday as financial markets in Japan will not reopen until Monday.
Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.3465/75 Swiss francs, up from 1.3445/55 francs at the open.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3755/60 from C$1.3712/17.
The Australian dollar closed at $0.7905/10, down from $0.7919/24 at the open.
